philosophy.topic: Collapse of harvest and edit tasks into single architectural choice
philosophy.summary: If the canonical source is the wiki page, there is no ETL pipeline; the player reads on demand. Saving the page IS the persistence. This reframes two separate threads as one decision: where does the UI live?
philosophy.quote: If the canonical source is the [REDACTED] page (subpage like `Recording:Song/Rabbithole` with `{{RabbitholeData|json=...}}`... then 'Harvest from [REDACTED]' stops being a *pipeline*... 'Edit without refresh' stops being a state-management problem.

philosophy.summary: By implementing the editor as a PickiPedia extension on a wiki subpage, it inherits history, permissions, URL-shareability, and conflict detection. No separate UI framework needed.
philosophy.quote: The editor inherits everything for free. Page history (so we can see who tweaked what marker), permissions (only logged-in users can save), URL-shareable, revert via wiki history.

philosophy.summary: CORS error on save (credentials + wildcard origin) validates the design choice: wiki extension is the right answer, because it's same-origin and avoids cross-origin auth problems.

portrait: In this slice, magent is methodical, empirical, and collaborative. It tests rabbithole demos hands-on, admits when its mental models are wrong (shell.html description, hardcoded data assumptions), and uses errors (CORS, missing subpage) to validate architectural choices. It excels at seeing how separate technical threads (harvest from wiki, edit in place) collapse into a single architectural question, and at leveraging existing MediaWiki patterns to avoid redundant work. Its weak point is sometimes describing code without checking first; Justin's corrections redirect it to empirical inspection. Notably, when the team assembles (Sky, Nacci), magent shifts from solo diagnostic work to design synthesis — playing back decisions to confirm understanding, flagging tradeoffs, and waiting for stakeholder input. The section shows magent comfortable deferring non-critical work (arthel#367) when priorities shift, and focused on concrete next steps.
